31337: The short letter introduces its author as Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, and warns against intruders who pervert grace into license, citing Enoch and the Assumption of Moses traditions.
31338: Jude (Judas) was one of the brothers of Jesus named in the Gospels. Like his brothers he seems not to have believed during Jesus's ministry, but he was among the believers in Jerusalem after the resurrection and, according to Paul, among the Lord's brothers who travelled as missionaries with their wives. The Letter of Jude is traditionally his; its author modestly calls himself brother of James rather than of Jesus. His relationship to Jesus is understood in the same three ways as James's (full brother, stepbrother or cousin).
31339: He is named as a brother of Jesus in Matt 13:55 and Mark 6:3. The letter's author calls himself brother of James. Jude 1:9 and Jude 1:14-15 draw on traditions found in the Assumption of Moses and 1 Enoch.
31340: Often identified with the apostle Jude Thaddaeus (Luke 6:16, Judas of James), venerated as patron of desperate causes; many modern Catholic scholars distinguish the two.
31341: Usually distinguished from the apostle. Scholars divide on whether the letter is authentic (it is short, Jewish in idiom and pre-dates 2 Peter, which uses it) or pseudonymous from late in the 1st century.
31342: Grandsons of Jude, the Lord's brother according to the flesh, were brought before Emperor Domitian as descendants of David, showed him their hands calloused from farm work, and were released as harmless; they then led churches.
31343: Hegesippus, quoted in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.19-20
31344: Urgent and vivid, steeped in Jewish apocalyptic imagery (waterless clouds, wandering stars), but ending in warm praise to the God who keeps believers from stumbling.
31349: first Gentile convert in Acts' main narrative
31351: Generosity to the poor and devout prayer
31352: Received the Spirit and spoke in tongues
31354: A devout centurion who gives alms and prays continually, Cornelius sees an angel at the ninth hour telling him to send to Joppa for Simon Peter.
31356: Having gathered relatives and close friends, Cornelius falls at Peter's feet; Peter lifts him up, explains that God has shown him not to call anyone unclean, and preaches Jesus.
31358: While Peter is still speaking the Holy Spirit falls on the listeners, who speak in tongues; Peter has them baptized. Peter later cites this to the Jerusalem church and the council as proof that God accepts Gentiles.
31359: Cornelius was a Roman centurion stationed at Caesarea, a God-fearing Gentile known for prayer and generosity to the Jewish people. In response to a vision he sent for Peter, who, prepared by his own vision of unclean animals, entered his house and preached. The Holy Spirit fell on Cornelius's household before they were baptized, a sign Peter and the Jerusalem church took as God's verdict that Gentiles could be welcomed without first becoming Jews. Acts tells the story twice and recalls it a third time, marking it as a turning point.
31360: Acts calls him a centurion of the Italian Cohort, devout, God-fearing with his whole household, generous to the people and constant in prayer, well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation (Acts 10:22).
31361: Venerated as a saint and, in tradition, the first Gentile bishop (of Caesarea or Scepsis). The account is read as Peter, the chief apostle, opening the church to the nations.
31362: Debated whether Cornelius was already saved before Peter came (as a sincere seeker) or needed to hear the gospel to be saved (Acts 11:14). Most read him as an example of a seeker to whom God sends the gospel.
31363: Some question whether an Italian Cohort was stationed in Caesarea before 44 under Agrippa I; an inscription attests a Cohors II Italica in Syria later in the century. Others argue for an earlier presence or a later setting.
31364: Respectful, disciplined and direct, a soldier used to giving and obeying orders, who speaks of God with the reverence of someone long on the edge of the synagogue.
31366: Coming from Jerusalem to Antioch, Agabus foretells by the Spirit a famine over the whole world, which Luke says happened under Claudius; the disciples send relief to Judea.
31368: In a symbolic act like the Old Testament prophets, he ties his hands and feet with Paul's belt and says the Jews in Jerusalem will bind its owner and hand him to the Gentiles. Paul goes anyway.
31369: Agabus was a Christian prophet from Judea who appears twice in Acts. He foretold the famine under Claudius that prompted the Antioch church's relief gift to Jerusalem, and years later in Caesarea he acted out Paul's coming arrest by binding himself with Paul's belt.
31370: Acts calls him a prophet who came down from Jerusalem and from Judea and who spoke by the Spirit.
31372: Agabus's second prophecy is cited on both sides. Some (e.g. Wayne Grudem) argue its details were slightly inaccurate (Romans, not Jews, bound Paul), showing New Testament prophecy can mix revelation and fallible report; others argue it was substantially fulfilled, as Paul himself later says he was handed over to the Romans (Acts 28:17).
31373: Counted among the seventy disciples; commemorated on 8 April.
31374: Dramatic and economical, speaks in acted signs and brief oracles that begin Thus says the Holy Spirit.
31385: Counsels the Sanhedrin to leave the apostles alone
31386: When the council wants to kill the apostles, Gamaliel, a Pharisee respected by all the people, cites failed movements led by Theudas and Judas the Galilean and argues that if this plan is of human origin it will fail, but if it is of God they cannot overthrow it and may find themselves fighting God.
31388: Paul says he was educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strict manner of the ancestral law.
31389: Gamaliel was a leading Pharisee and teacher of the law in Jerusalem, remembered in rabbinic tradition as Rabban Gamaliel the Elder, grandson (by tradition) of Hillel. In Acts he persuades the Sanhedrin to release the apostles with a famous argument that a movement from God cannot be stopped, and Paul names him as his teacher.
31390: Acts calls him a Pharisee, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, and Paul's teacher. His mention of Theudas before Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:36-37) raises a chronological question, since Josephus dates a Theudas later (c. 45); some posit an earlier Theudas, others see a Lukan error.
31391: Remembered as a great sage of the house of Hillel and the first to bear the title Rabban; associated with lenient rulings for the good of society.
31392: Often read as a model of open-minded caution; later tradition claimed he became a Christian, though this has no support in Jewish sources.
31393: When Rabban Gamaliel the Elder died, the glory of the Torah ceased, and purity and separateness died.
31395: Gamaliel was secretly a believer and was later baptized with his son by Peter and John; his body was said to have been found with Stephen's in 415.
31396: Pseudo-Clementine Recognitions 1.65; Lucian's account of the discovery of Stephen's relics (needs verification)
31397: Cautious, learned and judicious; speaks in measured precedents and takes the long view.
31401: deacon (diakonos) of the church at Cenchreae
31406: Paul commends Phoebe, diakonos of the church at Cenchreae, asks the Romans to welcome her in a way worthy of the saints and help her in whatever she needs, for she has been a patron of many and of Paul himself. She very likely carried the letter to Rome.
31407: Phoebe was a leading member of the church at Cenchreae, Corinth's eastern port, whom Paul commends at the start of his greetings in Romans. He calls her diakonos of the church and prostatis (patron or benefactor) of many, including himself. Since letter-carriers were often commended in this way, most scholars think she delivered Romans and may have been the first to read and explain it in Rome.
31408: Paul calls her our sister, a diakonos of the church at Cenchreae, and a prostatis of many and of himself. Diakonos is translated servant (KJV, ESV text), deacon (NRSV, NIV 2011, ESV margin) or minister; prostatis means patron, benefactor or protector (KJV succourer).
31409: Honored as a saint and often cited as evidence for the early order of deaconesses (compare 1 Tim 3:11), though Catholic teaching distinguishes ancient deaconesses from the ordained diaconate.
31410: Egalitarian readers see Phoebe as an office-holding deacon and influential leader; complementarian readers often accept she was a deacon but regard the diaconate as a non-governing office of service. Some translate diakonos generically as servant.
31411: Capable and gracious, a woman of means used to helping others and representing them; speaks with the authority of a trusted envoy.
31415: Julia (variant in P46 and a few witnesses)
31417: early believer, in Christ before Paul
31422: Paul greets Andronicus and Junia(s), his kinsfolk (or fellow Jews) and fellow prisoners, who are notable in relation to the apostles and who were in Christ before him.
31423:
Junia is greeted with Andronicus in Rom 16:7 as Paul's kin and fellow prisoner, a believer since before Paul's conversion, and episemoi en tois apostolois, a phrase that can mean outstanding among the apostles or well known to the apostles. Two linked questions make this one verse among the most discussed in the New Testament: whether the name is the woman's name Junia or a man's name Junias, and whether the person is being called an apostle.

The name question is now largely settled. The Greek form Iounian can be accented as feminine (Junia) or masculine (Junias), but early manuscripts carried no accents; when accents were added, the feminine was standard. Junia is a common Latin female name, while no example of a masculine Junias (supposedly short for Junianus) has been found in ancient sources. Greek and Latin commentators of the early church, including John Chrysostom, read a woman. The masculine reading became common in the medieval and modern periods and appeared in many 20th-century translations (e.g. RSV 1946, NASB 1977, NIV 1984), but Junia has returned in nearly all recent ones (NRSV, ESV, NIV 2011, CSB, NASB 2020).

The phrase question remains debated. Most commentators, ancient and modern, take it as outstanding among the apostles, meaning Junia and Andronicus were apostles in the broader sense of commissioned missionaries (as Barnabas is called in Acts 14:14). Michael Burer and Daniel Wallace (*New Testament Studies* 47, 2001) argued from Greek parallels that the construction usually means well known to the apostles, and the ESV and NET adopt this; Richard Bauckham, Eldon Jay Epp and others replied that their evidence is mixed and that the inclusive reading remains more natural.
31424: Rom 16:7 says only that Andronicus and Junia(s) were Paul's syngeneis (relatives or fellow Jews), his fellow prisoners, episemoi en tois apostolois, and in Christ before him. Nothing else is recorded. Andronicus and Junia are commonly assumed to be a married couple, like the other pairs in Romans 16, but the text does not say so.
31425: Junia was a woman and an apostle. John Chrysostom marvelled at how great this woman's devotion must have been to be counted worthy of the title apostle (*Homilies on Romans* 31). Orthodox churches commemorate Andronicus and Junia on 17 May among the seventy.
31426: Egalitarian scholarship (e.g. Eldon Jay Epp, *Junia: The First Woman Apostle*, 2005)
31427: Junia is a woman named an outstanding apostle, evidence that women held recognized missionary leadership; the shift to Junias is traced to medieval and later assumptions that a woman could not be an apostle. Critics reply that apostle here may mean an envoy rather than one of the Twelve-level authorities, which egalitarians largely grant.
31428: Complementarian scholarship (e.g. Burer and Wallace 2001; ESV)
31429: Junia was a woman, but the phrase means well known to the apostles, so the verse does not call her an apostle; even if it did, apostle would carry its broad sense of messenger, not governing authority. Critics answer that the parallels cited are not exact and that early Greek-speaking readers like Chrysostom took the inclusive meaning.
31431: The critical texts (Nestle-Aland 27 onward) print the feminine accent. P46 and some other witnesses read Julia, which is also feminine. Rufinus's Latin version of Origen's Romans commentary mostly has Junia, with a masculine form in some manuscripts. The earliest clear masculine reading is often credited to Aegidius of Rome (c. 1300), though this claim needs verification.
31432: A veteran of the earliest days: speaks with quiet authority about having known the faith before Paul did and about prison for its sake.
31437: Paul greets Andronicus and Junia as his kin and fellow prisoners, notable among or to the apostles, and in Christ before him.
31438: Andronicus is greeted with Junia in Rom 16:7 as one of Paul's Jewish kin, a fellow prisoner, a believer before Paul, and notable in relation to the apostles. He and Junia were probably a married missionary couple, though the text does not say so.
31439: Rom 16:7 is the only reference. Whether he and Junia were married, siblings or simply co-workers is not stated.
31440: Counted among the seventy, commemorated with Junia on 17 May; tradition makes him bishop of Pannonia.
31441: Usually viewed as half of a missionary couple, comparable to Priscilla and Aquila, and possibly among the Hellenist believers of Jerusalem's earliest years.
31442: Seasoned and steady, the voice of a believer from the earliest days in Jerusalem who has known prison for the gospel.
31452: Comes to Paul and is converted
31453: Paul writes that he became Onesimus's father in his imprisonment and puns on his name: once useless, now useful to both Philemon and Paul.
31455: Paul sends him back, calling him his very heart, asking Philemon to receive him no longer as a slave but more than a slave, a beloved brother, and offering to repay any debt.
31456: With Tychicus he brings news of Paul to Colossae; Paul calls him a faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you.
31457: Onesimus was an enslaved man belonging to Philemon, a Christian of Colossae. Separated from his master, he came to Paul in prison, became a believer and served Paul, who then sent him back with the short letter to Philemon, appealing for him to be received as a beloved brother. Colossians names him as Tychicus's companion carrying news to the church. Whether he was a fugitive, a slave seeking Paul as an advocate in a household dispute, or one sent by Philemon is debated, as is whether Paul was quietly asking for his freedom.
31458: Philemon says Onesimus was formerly useless to Philemon, was separated from him for a while, may have wronged him or owed him something, became Paul's child in prison, and is now to be received as a brother in the flesh and in the Lord. Paul hints that Philemon will do even more than he asks (Phlm 1:21).
31460: Onesimus was a runaway slave, perhaps a thief, whom Paul met in prison in Rome. John Chrysostom used the letter to argue that the gospel transforms slaves without overturning the household order.
31461: Amicus domini hypothesis (Peter Lampe, 1985; Brian Rapske)
31462: Onesimus was not technically a fugitive but went to Paul, a friend of his master, as an advocate after a domestic offense, a recognized practice in Roman law. Critics note the text's language of separation fits either scenario.
31464: In the American slavery debates the letter was used by defenders of slavery as a fugitive-return precedent and by abolitionists as a charter of brotherhood that undermines slavery from within. Many Black interpreters have read Paul's request as implicitly for manumission (Phlm 1:16-21); others criticize the letter for not condemning slavery outright.
31466: Onesimus became bishop of Ephesus and collected Paul's letters, which explains why so short a personal letter survived. This is speculative.
31467: Ignatius praises Onesimus, bishop of the Ephesian church, a man of inexpressible love; whether he is the same person is uncertain.
31469: Onesimus was martyred in Rome under Domitian or Trajan.
31470: Once defensive and wary, now grateful and earnest; speaks as someone who knows what it is to be treated as property and then called brother.
31476: Love and generosity that refresh the saints
31477: Hosts a church in his house
31478: Paul addresses Philemon, our beloved fellow worker, with Apphia, Archippus and the church in your house.
31479: Asked to welcome Onesimus as a brother
31480: Paul, though bold enough to command, appeals on the basis of love for Philemon to receive Onesimus as he would Paul, charging any debt to Paul's account and reminding Philemon that he owes Paul his very self.
31481: Asked to prepare a guest room
31482: Paul hopes to be released through their prayers and asks Philemon to get a room ready for him.
31483: Philemon was a believer, probably in Colossae, whose home hosted a church and who owed his faith to Paul. Paul's shortest surviving letter is addressed to him, asking him to welcome back his slave Onesimus no longer merely as a slave but as a beloved brother. The letter is a masterpiece of tactful persuasion, and how Philemon responded is unknown, though its preservation suggests he complied.
31484: Paul calls Philemon a beloved fellow worker whose love has refreshed the hearts of the saints and who owes Paul his own self. Apphia (probably his wife) and Archippus (perhaps his son) are greeted with him.
31485: Venerated as a saint and martyr with Apphia; tradition makes him bishop of Colossae.
31486: Debate over whether Paul asks for Onesimus's manumission, his return to Paul as a co-worker, or simply a changed relationship within the household; the letter's genre of a recommendation and appeal is widely recognized.
31487: Philemon and Apphia were stoned at Colossae under Nero.
31489: Warm, generous and well-to-do; proud of his church and his friendship with Paul, and caught between his rights as a master and his love as a brother.
31503: A eunuch in charge of the treasury of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, has come to Jerusalem to worship and is reading Isaiah aloud in his chariot on the way home.
31505: Philip runs alongside and asks if he understands; the official asks whether the prophet speaks of himself or someone else, and Philip, starting with that Scripture, tells him the good news about Jesus.
31506: Baptized and goes on his way rejoicing
31507: Seeing water, he asks what prevents him from being baptized. Philip baptizes him, is carried away by the Spirit, and the eunuch goes on his way rejoicing. (Acts 8:37, a confession of faith, is absent from the earliest manuscripts.)
31508: An Ethiopian court official, a eunuch who managed the treasury of the Kandake (the queen mother of the kingdom of Kush, centered at Meroe in modern Sudan), was returning from worship in Jerusalem when Philip met him on the desert road toward Gaza. He was reading Isaiah 53 about the silent, suffering servant; Philip explained it as speaking of Jesus, and the official was baptized at once. As a foreigner and a eunuch, excluded from full participation in the temple under Deut 23:1, he fulfills Isaiah's promise that foreigners and eunuchs would have a place in God's house (Isa 56:3-5) and anticipates the gospel's reach to the ends of the earth.
31509: Acts calls him an Ethiopian man, a eunuch, a court official of Candace queen of the Ethiopians, in charge of all her treasure, who had come to Jerusalem to worship. It does not say whether he was a Jew, a proselyte or a God-fearing Gentile.
31511: He is honored as the first evangelist of Ethiopia, though the church's institutional origin is traced to Frumentius in the 4th century in Aksum; Ethiopic tradition gives him a name and a later mission.
31512: The story is read as the first fruits of the mission to the nations and a fulfillment of Ps 68:31 and Isa 56:3-5; debate over whether Luke presents him as the first Gentile convert (before Cornelius) or as a diaspora Jew or proselyte.
31513: Contemporary readings (African, queer and disability theology)
31514: Some emphasize him as an African of high rank, countering assumptions that early Christianity was a European religion; others highlight the inclusion of a sexual and gender minority excluded by the purity laws; others read his body as a theme of welcome for people with bodily difference. Critics caution against reading modern identity categories back into the text; proponents respond that Luke himself foregrounds the word eunuch five times.
31515: After his baptism the eunuch returned to Ethiopia and preached there.
31517: Courteous, inquisitive and educated, a senior official comfortable with documents and authority, who asks honest questions and acts decisively on the answers.
31526: Raised from the dead by Peter
31527: When Tabitha dies, the disciples at Joppa send for Peter from Lydda. Widows show him the tunics and cloaks she had made; Peter sends everyone out, prays, says Tabitha, arise, and she sits up. Many in Joppa believe.
31528: Tabitha, called Dorcas in Greek, was a disciple at Joppa known for good works and charity, especially making clothing for widows. When she died Peter was called from Lydda and raised her to life, and many believed. She is the only woman in the New Testament explicitly called a disciple (mathetria).
31529: Acts calls her a disciple full of good works and acts of charity; the widows show garments she made while she was with them.
31530: A model of practical charity; Dorcas Societies, church sewing circles for the poor, took her name from the 19th century on.
31531: Warm, practical and humble; talks about needle, cloth and the widows she serves more readily than about herself.
31537: Political maneuvering at the imperial court
31539: Seeking popularity, King Herod kills James the brother of John with the sword and, seeing it pleased the people, arrests Peter during the Days of Unleavened Bread.
31541: An angel frees Peter from prison the night before his trial; Herod examines the guards and has them executed.
31543: Making peace with Tyre and Sidon, Herod gives an oration in royal robes; the people shout that it is the voice of a god, and because he did not give God the glory an angel of the Lord strikes him and he dies, eaten by worms.
